concepts.label: Event Context

misconceptions.claim: A SIEM automatically makes incomplete source events reliable.
misconceptions.correction: Correlation can expose patterns, but it cannot recover missing identity, inaccurate time, altered records, or an unmonitored source.
Retention must balance investigative value with privacy, access risk, cost, legal authority, and the ability to protect the records.

outcome: Given a service and its risks, select event sources, fields, time controls, retention, integrity protections, and egress visibility that produce actionable evidence.

sections.body: Start with an operational or investigative question: who changed a control, which identity accessed a record, what crossed an egress boundary, or which process made a decision. Select sources across identity, endpoint, application, database, network, cloud control plane, and physical systems. Record time, source, subject, object, action, result, correlation identifier, location, and relevant policy or device context. The collection decision balances detection value, performance, privacy, retention cost, and legal constraints. A verbose log with no stable identity, synchronized time, or outcome is not strong evidence.
keyPoints: Event selection follows risk and use cases, not a blanket collect-everything rule.
Context fields make events attributable and correlatable across systems.
Missing time, identity, outcome, or source integrity can make an event misleading.
sections.title: Choose events and context that answer a question

sections.body: Log management includes transport, normalization, storage, indexing, access control, integrity protection, retention, archival, disposal, and recovery. Synchronize clocks or record reliable offsets so a timeline can be reconstructed. Use append-oriented or otherwise tamper-evident storage, restrict administration, separate operators from investigators where appropriate, and monitor logging failures. Egress monitoring complements inbound detection by looking for unusual destinations, volume, protocol, identity, or data movement. Retention should satisfy investigative, regulatory, contractual, and privacy needs while defining what happens when storage, transport, or a source is unavailable.
keyPoints: A logging control must detect its own collection, transport, and storage failure.
Retention is a policy decision tied to use, law, and cost; indefinite retention is not automatically safer.
Egress signals need identity, asset, baseline, and data context to avoid treating normal synchronization as exfiltration.
sections.title: Protect logs and make retention defensible

summary: Logging architecture makes security-relevant activity observable, attributable, time-ordered, protected, and usable without collecting everything indiscriminately.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.

teaching.focalRelation: Preserve each raw timestamp; define signed offset as clock minus reference; compute corrected time as raw minus offset; expand corrected values by measured uncertainty; nonoverlapping intervals support only IdP before database before egress, while intent, causality, completeness, and any event with unknown offset remain unresolved.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Clock correction and uncertainty intervals can support temporal order when corrected ranges do not overlap. That order does not by itself prove causality, intent, or complete collection.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: Aligned corrected timestamps and uncertainty intervals let the learner compare ranges directly and see why order is supported while causality remains unproven.

treatmentDispositions.rationale: Implements the reviewed native offset timeline with raw and corrected timestamps side by side: IdP 10:00:00±2s [09:59:58,10:00:02]; DB raw 10:04:20 with signed +4:00 correction to 10:00:20±2s [10:00:18,10:00:22]; egress 10:00:40±2s [10:00:38,10:00:42]. The measured branch supports only IdP<DB<egress temporal order. The unknown-offset branch withdraws DB precedence while retaining IdP<egress, and both branches reject intent, causality, or completeness claims.

title: Build logging architecture that preserves useful evidence

workedExamples.reasoning: Correlate identity, role change, query, and egress events using stable identifiers and correct for clock offsets before drawing a timeline. Preserve the original records, restrict access, document the offset and collection gap, and avoid claiming intent from an incomplete sequence. Improve time synchronization and alert on privileged changes followed by sensitive egress.
workedExamples.situation: A privileged operator exports a customer dataset shortly after changing a database role. The database log has the query, the identity provider has the authentication, and the egress sensor sees an unusual destination, but clocks differ by four minutes.
workedExamples.takeaway: Correlate identity, role change, query, and egress events using stable identifiers and correct for clock offsets before drawing a timeline. Preserve the original records, restrict access, document the offset and collection gap, and avoid claiming intent from an incomplete sequence. Improve time synchronization and alert on privileged changes followed by sensitive egress.
